newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Puerto Rico blends Latin, U.S. cultures.
newsitem.headline: Puerto Rico blends Latin, U.S. cultures.

text.p: Is it like New Jersey or Caracas, Bogota or Boston, Havana or Hartford?

Retaining the culture of Puerto Rico has been at the centre of a raging debate over whether the island commonwealth, a U.S. possession for 99 years, should seek to become a full-fledged U.S. state -- a position espoused by Gov. Pedro Rossello's New Progressive Party, which won the majority of the island's political offices last fall.
On the one hand, advocates of statehood acknowledge it could be difficult to sell the idea of a Spanish-speaking state to most mainland Americans.
And on the other, many Puerto Ricans fear statehood would mean losing their Latin American identity, and being subsumed into the overwhelming U.S. culture of Hollywood, hamburgers and music videos.
But statehood advocates say the blend of cultures is already happening.
"Communications allow us to see things immediately. If there is some activity going on in a McDonald's in Chicago, we see it immediately," Gov. Pedro Rossello told Reuters.
The result is an island of what can be jarring cultural dissonances.

In the 500-year-old walled city of Old San Juan, a branch of the Atlanta-based Hooters restaurant chain known for waitresses in orange hot pants, sits just down the street from Fort San Cristobal, a stone fortress completed in 1772.

Narrow cobbled streets house a Hard Rock Cafe and T-shirt shops, as well as vendors hawking the flavored ices known as "piraguas," and the San Juan Cathedral, final resting place of the Spanish explorer Juan Ponce de Leon.

Further from the city centre, an ice cream truck bearing the products of the Vermont firm Ben & Jerry's pulls up to a supermarket, which lies a short distance from an arena used for cockfighting, a favourite sport of gamblers that is so popular there is a government office to monitor it.
Street signs mark distances in the metric measure kilometres and gasoline is sold in litres, but speed limits are given in U.S. miles-per-hour.
In one day, a lawyer can argue a case in federal court in English and another in a commonwealth court, where proceedings take place in Spanish.

Some in Puerto Rico also note that parts of the U.S. mainland can seem even more Latin American than the Caribbean island itself. "At least we speak English here, not like in Miami," one treasury official said.
